case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the hospital with fever, joint pain, and second-degree atrioventricular block. His medical history included several years of diffuse xanthomas of the skin, peripheral hypereosinophilia, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary nodules, bilateral anterior uveitis, avascular necrosis of the wrist, and IgG κ light chain monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. No diagnosis had been identified, and treatments had included corticosteroids and methotrexate. Physical examination revealed diffuse xanthomata most prominent in the periorbital region (Figure 1A) and multiple swollen and tender small joints in the hands and wrists. A 2 × 2-mm biopsy from the right periorbital lesion was obtained. Histopathologic features are shown inFigure 1B. There was no evidence of necrobiosis. Results ofBRAFimmunostaining were negative. κ and λ Stains by in situ hybridization showed rare scattered positively staining plasma cells. Laboratory studies demonstrated an absolute eosinophil count of 3180 cells/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; reference range, 0-400 cells/μL) and normal lipid panel results; testing results for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level was normal. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed lucencies in the right parietal bone and fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the right iliac bone, bone marrow, spleen, cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules, and multiple axillary, thoracic, and pelvic lymph nodes. Biopsies of the bone marrow and a subcarinal lymph node demonstrated aKRASG12D gene alteration.
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of periorbital xanthomas. B, Diffuse lipid-laden foamy histiocytes (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of periorbital xanthomas. B, Diffuse lipid-laden foamy histiocytes (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:

       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.

     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

case_info.explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

case_info.explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 60s presented to the hospital with fever, joint pain, and second-degree atrioventricular block. His medical history included several years of diffuse xanthomas of the skin, peripheral hypereosinophilia, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary nodules, bilateral anterior uveitis, avascular necrosis of the wrist, and IgG κ light chain monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. No diagnosis had been identified, and treatments had included corticosteroids and methotrexate. Physical examination revealed diffuse xanthomata most prominent in the periorbital region (Figure 1A) and multiple swollen and tender small joints in the hands and wrists. A 2 × 2-mm biopsy from the right periorbital lesion was obtained. Histopathologic features are shown inFigure 1B. There was no evidence of necrobiosis. Results ofBRAFimmunostaining were negative. κ and λ Stains by in situ hybridization showed rare scattered positively staining plasma cells. Laboratory studies demonstrated an absolute eosinophil count of 3180 cells/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; reference range, 0-400 cells/μL) and normal lipid panel results; testing results for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level was normal. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed lucencies in the right parietal bone and fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the right iliac bone, bone marrow, spleen, cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules, and multiple axillary, thoracic, and pelvic lymph nodes. Biopsies of the bone marrow and a subcarinal lymph node demonstrated aKRASG12D gene alteration.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."

Physical examination revealed diffuse xanthomata most prominent in the periorbital region (Figure 1A) and multiple swollen and tender small joints in the hands and wrists. A 2 × 2-mm biopsy from the right periorbital lesion was obtained. Histopathologic features are shown inFigure 1B. There was no evidence of necrobiosis. Results ofBRAFimmunostaining were negative. κ and λ Stains by in situ hybridization showed rare scattered positively staining plasma cells. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed lucencies in the right parietal bone and fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the right iliac bone, bone marrow, spleen, cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules, and multiple axillary, thoracic, and pelvic lymph nodes. Biopsies of the bone marrow and a subcarinal lymph node demonstrated aKRASG12D gene alteration.

case_info.explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

case_info.explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

next reply.

[Persona]

- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 8.1. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:

case_info.explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

A man in his 60s presented to the hospital with fever, joint pain, and second-degree atrioventricular block. His medical history included several years of diffuse xanthomas of the skin, peripheral hypereosinophilia, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary nodules, bilateral anterior uveitis, avascular necrosis of the wrist, and IgG κ light chain monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. No diagnosis had been identified, and treatments had included corticosteroids and methotrexate. Physical examination revealed diffuse xanthomata most prominent in the periorbital region (Figure 1A) and multiple swollen and tender small joints in the hands and wrists. A 2 × 2-mm biopsy from the right periorbital lesion was obtained. Histopathologic features are shown inFigure 1B. There was no evidence of necrobiosis. Results ofBRAFimmunostaining were negative. κ and λ Stains by in situ hybridization showed rare scattered positively staining plasma cells. Laboratory studies demonstrated an absolute eosinophil count of 3180 cells/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; reference range, 0-400 cells/μL) and normal lipid panel results; testing results for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level was normal. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed lucencies in the right parietal bone and fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the right iliac bone, bone marrow, spleen, cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules, and multiple axillary, thoracic, and pelvic lymph nodes. Biopsies of the bone marrow and a subcarinal lymph node demonstrated aKRASG12D gene alteration.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
